content:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is diagnosed by a rheumatologist, based on your symptoms, an examination of your joints, blood tests and sometimes scans. There is no single test that proves or rules out RA. If your GP finds persistent joint swelling, NICE says you should be referred urgently to rheumatology, even if your blood tests are normal.

Step 1: seeing your GP

Your GP will ask about:

  • which joints are painful or swollen, and whether both sides are affected
  • how long morning stiffness lasts. More than 30 minutes suggests inflammation.
  • how long symptoms have lasted
  • tiredness, weight loss or feeling unwell
  • family history of RA or other autoimmune conditions
  • smoking

They will examine your joints, looking for swelling, warmth and tenderness, especially in the small joints of the hands and feet. A positive "squeeze test", where squeezing across the knuckles or the balls of the feet causes pain, can suggest inflammation.

Related reading: What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?, Best Exercise for Rheumatoid Arthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment

Step 2: blood tests

Your GP may arrange tests including:

  • CRP and ESR: measure inflammation in the body
  • rheumatoid factor (RF): an antibody found in many people with RA, but also in some healthy people and other conditions
  • anti-CCP antibodies: more specific to RA. A positive result makes RA more likely and may suggest more active disease.
  • full blood count, kidney and liver function: to check general health and help plan treatment

Many people with RA have positive RF or anti-CCP, but not all. A negative result does not rule out RA. This is called "seronegative" RA.

Step 3: referral to rheumatology

NICE (NG100) recommends urgent referral for adults with suspected persistent synovitis of undetermined cause. Refer urgently if:

  • the small joints of the hands or feet are affected
  • more than one joint is affected
  • there has been a delay of three months or longer between symptoms starting and seeking advice

Your GP should not wait for blood test results if they find persistent joint swelling. If you are waiting, ask your GP about pain relief and what to do if things get worse.

Step 4: assessment by a rheumatologist

The rheumatologist will take a detailed history, examine your joints and review tests. They may arrange:

  • X-rays of hands and feet, to look for early damage and to provide a baseline
  • ultrasound, which can show inflammation not obvious on examination
  • MRI occasionally

They will consider other conditions that can look similar, such as psoriatic arthritis, lupus, viral arthritis, gout and polymyalgia rheumatica.

Classification criteria

Rheumatologists may use criteria that score joint involvement, blood tests, inflammation levels and symptom duration. These help with research and consistency, but diagnosis is ultimately based on the rheumatologist's clinical judgement.

After diagnosis

If RA is confirmed, treatment usually begins straight away with a disease-modifying medicine such as methotrexate, sometimes with a short course of steroids. You should be offered:

  • information about RA and your treatment
  • a named contact or advice line
  • access to physiotherapy, occupational therapy and podiatry
  • regular reviews until your disease is controlled

Preparing for appointments

  • write down your symptoms and when they started
  • note how long morning stiffness lasts
  • take photos of swollen joints
  • list your medicines, including over-the-counter products
  • bring questions and someone to support you if you wish

If you are told it is not RA

Sometimes symptoms settle, or another diagnosis is made. If symptoms return or change, go back to your GP. Some people develop RA over time after early, unclear symptoms.

Coping while you wait

Waiting for a diagnosis can be stressful. Keep moving gently, use the pain relief your GP or pharmacist recommends, and note any changes. If new joints become swollen or you feel much worse, contact your GP, as your referral may need to be upgraded.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
